pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 8–9y; apply the commutative, associative and distributive properties as STRATEGIES to multiply and divide (not as formal named laws to memorise).
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y4 'recognise and use factor pairs and commutativity', 'multiply … three numbers' (associativity), and use the distributive law within written/mental methods; Y3 begins distributive partitioning.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 3.OA.5 — 'Apply properties of operations as strategies to multiply and divide' (commutative: 6×4=4×6; associative: 2×(3×5) via (2×3)×5; distributive: 8×5+8×2 = 8×7). Note CCSS says pupils need not know the property names.
• Operational details — the point is flexible, efficient calculation: commutativity halves facts to learn and lets you reorder; associativity lets you regroup three factors into an easy pair (2×3×5 → 6×5 or 2×15); distributivity is the big one — split a hard fact/large factor into friendly parts (8×7 = 8×5 + 8×2) and it is the conceptual seed of the area model and ALL formal written multiplication. Show each property in the array/area model where it is visibly true, then use it to make calculation easier. Division is NOT commutative or associative — make that explicit.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 8): use commutativity (know 4×6 → 6×4) and split a fact distributively with support (7×6 = 5×6 + 2×6). Tier B (age 8–9): use all three to simplify a calculation and justify with an array. Tier C (age 9): choose the most efficient property for a given calculation and explain why division isn't commutative.
bestPractices: Prove each property visually first — rotate an array for commutativity, regroup counters for associativity, split an array for distributivity — then use it to make a calculation easier, so properties are tools not vocabulary.

Lead with the distributive property as the highest-value strategy: it turns unknown facts into known ones (8×7 = 8×5 + 8×2) and is the direct bridge to the area model and formal written multiplication.
Use the area model as the shared home of all three properties so the later written algorithm is 'properties made compact', not a new trick.
Explicitly contrast × (commutative/associative) with ÷ (neither) using counterexamples so children don't overgeneralise.
Prioritise strategy CHOICE — give calculations where different properties are most efficient and discuss which to pick.
keyRepresentations: Rotatable array — commutativity (same array, two orientations, same total)
Split area model — distributivity (8×7 as 8×5 + 8×2 two sub-rectangles)
Bar model / number sentence chains showing the equivalent forms
commonMisconceptions: Applying the distributive split incorrectly — e.g. 8×7 = 8×5 + 2 (forgetting to multiply the second part) or splitting the wrong factor.
Treating the properties as names to memorise rather than strategies to use, so they aren't deployed in calculation.
Not seeing that the area model IS the distributive law, so written multiplication later feels disconnected.
Thinking reordering changes the answer, or conversely that any reordering is always allowed.

learn.summary: For ages 8–9, teach the commutative, associative and distributive properties as calculation STRATEGIES (not named laws to memorise) that leave a total invariant. Prove each property visibly in an array/area model first, then use it to make a hard calculation easy. Centre the distributive split (8×7 = 8×5 + 8×2) as the highest-value strategy and the direct bridge to the area model and formal written multiplication. Explicitly contrast × (commutative/associative) with ÷ and − (neither), and prioritise strategy choice — which property is most efficient for a given calculation.

activities.title: Property playground: rotate, split, regroup on one array
feedback: If a learner writes 8×7 = 8×5 + 2 = 42, draw 8 rows of 7, cut into 8 rows of 5 and 8 rows of 2, and ask how many squares are in the second block: it is 8×2 = 16, not 2, so 40 + 16 = 56. Make the split visible before returning to symbols.

If a learner distrusts regrouping and recomputes (2×3)×4 and 2×(3×4) separately each time, build both with cubes (e.g. 4 lots of a 2-by-3 group, which is 6 taken 4 times, versus 2 lots of 12, where 12 is 3×4), count once each (24 both times), and name associativity as 'regrouping a multiplication never changes the total'.

If a learner says order 'doesn't matter' for division or subtraction (e.g. 8−7 = 7−8), show quick counterexamples such as 10−3 = 7 while 3−10 cannot be done with whole numbers (it goes below zero on a number line), and 12÷3 = 4 while 3÷12 is less than 1, so the property stays bound to × and + specifically.
Prompt justification: 'You said 8×5 + 8×2 — why is that the same as 8×7 and not more or less?' and 'Could you use 8×5 to help work out 8×9? Show me the split.'
activities.rationale: For multiplication, these properties are transformations that leave the total invariant, so letting a learner rotate, split and regroup while a live total holds is intended to help them discover each property rather than be told it, and immediately use it to simplify a calculation. A visible split-array is the area model, which embodies the distributive property and bridges to written multiplication. A division mode in which swapping the numbers changes the answer directly addresses the common overgeneralisation of commutativity to division. Dragging, live recolouring and the equal-total display are concrete examples of how the mechanism is made felt, not required implementations.
sourceClaims: Y4 pupils recognise and use factor pairs and commutativity, multiply three numbers, and use distributive partitioning within methods.
3.OA.5 requires applying commutative, associative and distributive properties as strategies to multiply and divide; pupils need not know the property names.
The area model embodies the distributive law and bridges to formal written multiplication; properties should be shown in arrays before being used as calculation strategies.
learnerActions: On an array/area canvas, meet an 'ugly' fact like 8×7. Drag a divider through the 7 to carve the array into 8×5 and 8×2; watch the two sub-rectangles light up as 40 and 16 and combine to 56.
Rotate the same array 90° and confirm the total does not change (8×7 = 7×8) — commutativity as 'same array, two orientations, same total'.
For three factors (2×3×5), toggle or drag the bracket between (2×3)×5 and 2×(3×5), and confirm the total holds — associativity as regrouping into an easier pair (6×5 or 2×15).

Switch to a division mode: swap the two numbers in a ÷ calculation (e.g. 32÷8 = 4 becomes 8÷32, which is less than 1) and see that the answer changes, then say in your own words why division is not commutative (32÷8 is not 8÷32).
Choose your own split for a new ugly fact (e.g. 8×9 = 8×5 + 8×4) and check the partial products add to the whole (40 + 32 = 72).
activities.intendedInsight: In multiplication, reordering, regrouping and splitting change how a calculation is written without changing its total; a hard multiplication fact can be cut into two friendly facts and reassembled. This 'cut-the-hard-one-into-two-easy-ones' move is the distributive property, and it is the same move that formal written multiplication later makes compact. Division and subtraction are not commutative or associative, so swapping or regrouping their numbers can change the answer.

activities.title: Split-area anchor for the distributive fact
feedback: If the learner cannot explain the invariance, point to the shared height (8) across both parts and the widths adding to 7 (5 + 2), so no squares are added or lost.
Connect the picture back to symbols: the whole rectangle's area is the sum of the two parts' areas.
activities.rationale: A fixed, pre-split area diagram is a clean anchor for the distributive idea and the area-model bridge. Because it cannot be moved to vary the split, it shows one case rather than invariance across many, so it supports rather than replaces manipulable exploration; use it as a static anchor or consolidation after the playground.
sourceClaims: The area model embodies the distributive law and bridges to formal written multiplication; properties should be shown in arrays before being used as calculation strategies.
learnerActions: Study an area rectangle for 8×7 that is pre-split into 8×5 and 8×2.
Reveal the labels: left part '8×5 = 40', right part '8×2 = 16', whole '= 56'.
Answer the prompt 'Why does splitting the 7 into 5 and 2 not change the total?' before moving on.
activities.intendedInsight: The distributive split keeps the whole fixed because the two sub-rectangles together are exactly the original rectangle; 8×7 and 8×5 + 8×2 name the same quantity.

activities.title: Consolidate and sort: valid forms and the division trap
feedback: For the fill-in, if the learner writes anything other than 2, return to the array: the second part must be 8 rows of 2, i.e. 8×2.
If the learner picks a division distractor for 6×4, remind them commutativity is about reordering the SAME operation, and test the division claim with small numbers (e.g. 6÷4 ≠ 4÷6).
When sorting, have the learner give a counterexample for each 'not true for ÷' statement (e.g. 32÷8 = 4 but 8÷32 is less than 1; (24÷4)÷2 = 3 but 24÷(4÷2) = 12).
activities.rationale: Completing a split, selecting the correct equivalent form and sorting always-true versus division statements target the overgeneralisation misconception. These checks assess and consolidate property USE; they do not by themselves build the invariance intuition, so pair them with the manipulable or anchor activities.
learnerActions: Choose which expression equals 6×4, with 4×6 correct and 6÷4 and 4÷6 offered as tempting wrong choices.
Sort statements into 'always true' versus 'not true for division', e.g. is 32÷8 = 8÷32? Is (24÷4)÷2 = 24÷(4÷2)?
activities.intendedInsight: Property use can be checked and the overgeneralisation to division can be caught: reordering and regrouping hold for × but not for ÷.

activities.title: The lazy mathematician: justify the easiest strategy
feedback: Push for reasons, not just answers: 'Is there an easier way to work that out, and how do you know it gives the same total?'
If the learner accepts an invalid division or subtraction reorder, ask them to test it with a concrete counterexample.
activities.rationale: A Socratic 'is there an easier way?' dialogue prompts strategy choice and verbal justification, which supports deployment of the properties. Discussion complements rather than substitutes for seeing the properties as visual transformations, so use it alongside the array work.
learnerActions: Talk with a 'lazy mathematician' character who always wants the easiest split or reorder for a given calculation.
When the character proposes a move (e.g. regroup 2×3×5 to 6×5, or split 7×6 into 5×6 + 2×6), explain why it gives the same answer.
Decide together which property is most efficient for different calculations and say why.
Catch the character out when it tries to 'reorder' a division or subtraction.
activities.intendedInsight: Choosing the most efficient property and justifying it out loud is part of fluent calculation; not every operation permits reordering.

constraints: Teach these as strategies for efficient calculation, not as formal named laws to memorise; CCSS-M notes pupils need not know the property names.
Make explicit that division is NOT commutative or associative, and that subtraction is not either; use counterexamples so learners do not overgeneralise.
Guard against the additive-split error (8×7 = 8×5 + 2): both parts must be multiplied by the shared factor (8×5 + 8×2).

The static split-area anchor and the sort/fill tasks check and consolidate property use, but a fixed diagram cannot vary the split or regrouping across many cases; manipulable exploration across varied cases can let learners meet the invariance across many instances, so pair the static anchor and check tasks with it.
Recognition and fill-in tasks assess property use; they do not themselves elicit the learner independently choosing and justifying a strategy, which the dialogue and open splits target.
Three-factor associativity can suggest a cuboid, but that belongs to volume; keep properties-as-strategies work in planar arrays/area to avoid added manipulation cost and off-topic meaning.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source labels a 3D treatment as adding 'no invariance insight'; this rewrite keeps the planar focus as a scoped design choice (arrays/area are where these properties are most directly visible) rather than a universal claim that 3D cannot teach anything here.

Arithmetic checked: 8×7 = 56; 8×5 = 40, 8×2 = 16, 40+16 = 56; 8×9 = 72 via 8×5 + 8×4 = 40 + 32; 2×3×5 = 30 via 6×5 or 2×15; 6×4 = 24 = 4×6; (24÷4)÷2 = 3 but 24÷(4÷2) = 12; 32÷8 = 4 but 8÷32 < 1. The additive-split error 8×5 + 2 = 42 appears only as a misconception to correct, never as a valid alternative.
The source mentions 'double 8×3.5' in passing for 8×7; this involves a non-integer partial and is not appropriate for this age group, so it is omitted from learner-facing actions.
The assessment's responseLevels, diagnosticPrompt and probe questions were not altered by this rewrite; they inform but are not restated as separate guidance fields.

Efficacy wording in constraint 4 was softened from 'is what lets learners feel the invariance' to a qualified affordance, since no source establishes manipulation as the necessary mechanism for building the invariance intuition.

probeDeeper: You said 8×5 + 8×2. Why is that the same as 8×7 and not more or less?
What if it had been 8 × 9 — could you use 8 × 5 to help? Show me the split.
Does this trick also work for 8 − 7? Why or why not?
Someone says 6 × 7 = 6×5 + 2. What went wrong in their thinking?
assess.correctAnswer: 8 × 7 = 56. A child reasoning correctly splits the 7: 8 × 7 is 8 × 5 plus 8 × 2, so 40 + 16 = 56 — because seven groups of eight is the same as five groups of eight and two more groups of eight (distributive property). Any valid split (8×7 = 8×6+8, or double 8×3.5 is not expected here) counts if the REASON is about decomposing one factor into parts that are added.

errorPatterns.pattern: treats distributive split additively on both parts: '8×7 = 8×5 + 2 = 42' — adds the leftover 2 instead of 8×2
errorPatterns.nextMove: draw the array: 8 rows of 7, cut it into 8 rows of 5 and 8 rows of 2; ask how many squares are in the second block — it is 8×2=16, not 2. Make the split visible before returning to symbols.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child gets 42 and, when probed, says 'I had 8×5 then added the 2 more'

errorPatterns.pattern: believes changing the grouping changes the answer — does not trust that (2×3)×4 = 2×(3×4); recomputes each time as if they could differ
errorPatterns.nextMove: build both groupings with cubes (2 stacks of 3, taken 4 times vs 2 stacks of 12) and count once each; name associativity as 'regrouping never changes the total'.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: when asked if reordering/regrouping factors is 'allowed', child hedges or checks by full recomputation rather than asserting it must be equal

errorPatterns.pattern: over-generalises commutativity/associativity to subtraction or division: 'if 8×7=7×8 then 8−7=7−8'
errorPatterns.nextMove: confront with a quick counterexample (10−3 vs 3−10 using a number line) so the property is bound to × and + specifically, not to all operations.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child asserts order 'doesn't matter' for a subtraction or division example

responseLevels.gap: gives 56 only by recomputing or recall, or gets 42 via the additive-split error; cannot explain why decomposing a factor is valid.
responseLevels.full: decomposes a factor and adds the partial products, justifies it as breaking the groups into parts that recombine to the whole (distributive), and transfers the strategy to a new fact (e.g. 8×9 via 8×5+8×4); correctly refuses to apply it to subtraction.
responseLevels.partial: correctly derives 56 from 8×5 and 8×2 for this case but treats it as a one-off trick — cannot generalise the split to a new factor or name why it must work.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: I know that 8 × 5 = 40. Without working out 8 × 7 the long way, can you use what you already know to figure it out? Tell me what you did and why it works.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who merely memorises facts can state 56 but cannot justify deriving it and will say 'I just know it' or recompute from scratch. A child who holds the property explains WHY 8×5+8×2 must equal 8×7 — the split of the factor, not luck. The reason-tier separates fact-recall from structural understanding, and the classic distributive error (adding to the wrong factor, or 8×7 = 8×5+2) surfaces here.
